Physicists May Have Found New Fundamental Particle Of Nature

TL;DR: There is almost certainly no new particle.

Alright guys, nobody get their hopes up. This article has almost no information, so here are the actual presentations given at the conference. Don't feel bad if you can't find the results that the article above is talking about. Each presentation devotes 2 slides out of ~55ish to this "new fundamental particle". In fact, none of the presentations even use the phrase "new fundamental particle". What gives?

1) The result is low statistical significance, 2 sigma for Atlas and 1.2 sigma for CMS (the two different detectors). Nobody should believe 2 sigma results. Did you know that the number of republicans in the US congress correlates with the solar neutrino flux at the 2 sigma level? 2 sigma BS is all over the place if you look hard enough. These scientists are looking REAL hard so they're bound to find some weird statistical flukes. The CERN scientists know this all to well (remember super-luminal neutrinos?), so they are very conservative about their statements (unlike the press).

2) If you accept the Higgs discovery, this "particle" (almost) can't be real. This is a bit of a technical point, but new particles which couple to the Electro-Weak interaction (i.e. can decay into photons like this new "particle") are constrained by what we have measured for the Higgs particle mass. The observed Higgs mass of ~127 GeV means that there are guaranteed to be no new particles which couple to the EW sector below a mass of ~(a few) TeV. The (much higher statistical significance) measurement of the Higgs mass directly conflicts with the inferred mass of this new particle at ~750GeV.

3) The only way to reconcile this new particle with the Higgs is to balance the Universe on the head of a pin. You can invent a zoo of new particles which contribute to the Higgs mass in such a way that the correction from this new "particle" is exactly cancelled out. Essentially, all the new particles at high energy need to be arranged just so, such that the mass of the Higgs boson is exactly what you would have measured if all those new particles had not existed at all.

4) It can't be evidence for the break down of the standard model of physics. Why? Everything else they found in other channels and at higher energies was entirely as predicted by the SM. All of the ways one might conceivably break the SM to allow for this particle to co-exist with the observed Higgs mass would also necessarily cause all of the other particle production channels at high energies to go hay-wire simultaneously. This is directly ruled out by the rest of the data.

For curiosity and interest!

The most intriguing result so far, reported on Tuesday, is an excess of pairs of gamma rays corresponding to an energy of about 750 billion electron volts. The gamma rays, the physicists said, could be produced by the radioactive decay of a new particle, in this case perhaps a cousin of the Higgs boson, which itself was first noticed because it decayed into an abundance of gamma rays.

Or it could be a more massive particle that has decayed in steps down to a pair of photons. Nobody knows. No model predicted this, which is how some scientists like it.

Great question. The Pentaquark is not so much a new particle as it is a newly observed bound state of known particles (quarks). The language in the particle physics community is a bit confusing due to the history of the field. There is an entire menagerie of mesons that where initially considered "new particles" and named accordingly prior to the discovery of the quarks. However, once the theory of the strong interaction was developed it became apparent that the Pion, Kaon, J/Psi particle, etc. were all simply different configurations of two quark bound states and not fundamental particles. It is still conventional to call such things particles but they are not "fundamental" particles as they are made of a composite of quarks.
